This is more fitting to be a clarification of an excuse than a rebuke. As for His saying «إني أعظك أن تكون من الجاهلين», what is meant by it is the prohibition against making the request in the future after Allah has informed him of the inner state of the matter, and that if the request occurred in the future he would be among the ignorant. The aim of that is to present what keeps him on the mark of infallibility, and exhortation does not require the occurrence of a sin. Nūḥ was apprehensive at his having ventured to ask his Lord about what he had not been given permission for, and feared destruction from that, so he took refuge with his Lord, was humble before Him, called upon Him and asked Him for forgiveness and mercy, because the good deeds of the righteous are the evil deeds of those brought near.

dervis-irab:77-83.t:
* Vocabulary:
(سِيءَ بِهِمْ): its original form is suwiʾa bihim, from al-sūʾ (evil); the wāw was made quiescent and its kasra was transferred to the sīn. One says "sūʾtuhu, so sīʾa", as one says "shaghaltuhu, so shughila" and "sarartuhu, so surra".
(ذَرْعاً): among their sayings is "so-and-so's dhirʿ was straitened". Al-dhirʿ is put in the place of capacity; the origin is that the camel measures with its forelegs in its walking, a measure (dhirʿ) according to the width of its stride; so when a load beyond its capacity is placed on it, its dhirʿ is straitened for that, it weakens and stretches out its neck. So narrowness of the dhirʿ became an expression for narrowness of capacity and ability. The meaning of His words «and he was straitened for them in dhirʿ» (وضاق بهم ذرعا) is that he found no escape from that unwelcome situation. Some scholars of the language said: its meaning is "his heart and breast were straitened for them", and its origin is not known unless it is said that al-dhirʿ is a metonym for capacity; the Arabs say "this is not in my hand", meaning "it is not in my capacity", because the forearm (dhirāʿ) is part of the hand. Others said: it is said "so-and-so was straitened in dhirʿ by such-and-such" when he fell into something unpleasant and cannot bear to get out of it.
In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj, in summary: "Al-dhirʿ is a verbal noun: the stretching out of the hand. 'Ḍuqtu bi-l-amr dhirʿan' means I was unable to cope with it; 'he is wide in dhirʿ' means capable; and 'he is empty of dhirʿ' means his heart is free of worries and griefs."
(يُهْرَعُونَ): that is, some of them drive others. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "hurʿa and uhriʿa, both passive, when he is made to hurry." In al-Qāmūs: "al-hara (with vowelled letters, and like ghurāb) and al-ihrāʿ is walking in agitation and haste; 'he came yuhraʿu' (with ḍamma) and 'uhriʿa' (passive) so he is muhraʿ, trembling from anger or fear; 'he has hariʿa' (like fariḥa); and 'a man hariʿ' is one quick to weep."
(عَصِيبٌ): al-ʿaṣīb is severe, especially in evil. Its origin is from tightening; one says "ʿaṣabtu al-shayʾ" meaning I tightened it, and "ʿaṣabtu the thigh of the she-camel" so that she would let her milk down, and a "ʿaṣūb she-camel". "A ʿaṣīb day" and "ʿaṣabṣab" is as if it wrapped itself around the people with evil, or its evil is wrapped together part upon part. The poet said:
فإنك إن لم ترض بكر بن وائل ... يكن لك يوم بالعراق عصيب
(For if you do not satisfy Bakr ibn Wāʾil, you will have a dire day in Iraq.)
And the rajaz poet said:
يوم عصيب ويعصب الأبطالا ... عصب القوي السلم الطوالا
(A dire day, that binds the heroes, the way the strong binds the long salam [trees].) [Translator's note: the meaning of the second hemistich is uncertain; the gloss is tentative.]
(رُكْنٍ): al-rukn is the support of a building after the foundation; the two rukns of a mountain are its two sides. The rajaz poet said:
يأوي إلى ركن من الأركان ... في عدد طلس ومجد بان
(He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, among many [companions] and an established glory.) [Translator's note: the gloss of عدد طلس is tentative.]
(فَأَسْرِ): from asrā in the sense of sarā, i.e. he travelled by night. Al-Nābigha said:
أسرت عليه من الجوزاء سارية ... تزجي الشمال عليه جامد البرد
(A night-travelling cloud from al-Jawzāʾ moved over it, the north wind driving upon it frozen hail.)
It is also transmitted as "sarat". And Imruʾ al-Qays said:
سريت بهم حتى تكل مطيهم ... وحتى الجياد ما يقدن بأرسان
(I travelled by night with them until their mounts grew weary, and even the steeds were no longer led by halters.)
(سِجِّيلٍ): Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is said that it is an Arabicized word from sang-kil, by the evidence of His words 'stones of clay'; and it is said it is from asjalahu, when he sent it, because it is sent upon the wrongdoers; and it is said it is from what Allah decreed to punish with, from al-sijill, as in 'sijill for so-and-so'." Abū ʿUbayda said: "It is hard stones", and he recited a verse of Ibn Muqbil:
ورجلة يضربون البيض ضاحية ... ضربا تواصى به الأبطال سجينا
(And foot soldiers who strike the helmets in the open, a blow that the heroes urged one another to, sijjīn.)
"Sijjīn and sijjīl are of one meaning, and the Arabs interchange nūn and lām, so here the nūn was changed into lām." The author of al-Qāmūs was satisfied with his words: "al-sijjīl is dry clay."
(مَنْضُودٍ): piled one upon another; al-naḍd is putting things one on top of another. What is meant is to describe the stones as abundant.
(مُسَوَّمَةً): marked for punishment; al-taswīm is the mark.

* I'rab:
(وَلَمَّا جاءَتْ رُسُلُنا لُوطاً سِيءَ بِهِمْ وَضاقَ بِهِمْ ذَرْعاً): لما is temporal or connective; جاءت رسلنا لوطا: a verb, an agent and a direct object; the clause سيء بهم has no grammatical position; the deputy agent refers back to Lūṭ; بهم is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to it; and ذرعا is a tamyīz transformed from the agent. (وَقالَ هذا يَوْمٌ عَصِيبٌ): وقال is conjoined to ضاق; هذا is a mubtadaʾ; يوم a khabar and عصيب an adjective, and the sentence is the reported speech. (وَجاءَهُ قَوْمُهُ يُهْرَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ): the wāw is a conjunction; جاءه قومه: a verb, a direct object and an agent; the clause يهرعون is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl; and إليه is attached to يهرعون. (وَمِنْ قَبْلُ كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ السَّيِّئاتِ): the wāw is circumstantial; من قبل: من is a preposition and قبل an adverbial indeclinable on the ḍamma because it is cut off from annexation in wording but not in meaning, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to يعملون; kāna and its ism; and the clause يعملون السيئات is the khabar of كانوا. (قالَ يا قَوْمِ هؤُلاءِ بَناتِي هُنَّ أَطْهَرُ لَكُمْ): هؤلاء is a mubtadaʾ and بناتي a khabar, and likewise His words هن أطهر لكم; they allowed بناتي to be a badal or an ʿaṭf bayān; هن is a separation pronoun with no position; أطهر is the khabar of هؤلاء; and لكم is attached to أطهر because it is an elative. An objection does not apply, the gist of which is that the elative implies sharing so that preference is valid, and so it would require that what they seek from men is pure; the answer is that this proceeds like «Is that better as a hospitality, or the tree of al-Zaqqūm?» (أذلك خير نزلا أم شجرة الزقوم), and it is known that there is no good at all in the tree of al-Zaqqūm. (فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَلا تُخْزُونِ فِي ضَيْفِي): the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; اتقوا الله: an imperative verb, an agent and a direct object; ولا تخزوني is conjoined to اتقوا الله; لا is prohibitive; تخزوني is jussive by لا, its sign of jussive being the deletion of the nūn; the nūn is for protection, the wāw is the agent and the yāʾ is a direct object; في ضيفي is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted ḥāl. Al-ḍayf is originally a maṣdar, then it was applied to one who comes at night to the host, therefore it applies to masculine and feminine, singular, dual and plural; it can be dualized, so one says ḍayfān, and pluralized, so one says aḍyāf, ḍuyūf and ḍīfān. (أَلَيْسَ مِنْكُمْ رَجُلٌ رَشِيدٌ): the interrogative is for denunciation and reproach; ليس is an incomplete past verb; منكم is the fronted khabar of ليس; رجل is its postponed ism; and رشيد an adjective. (قالُوا: لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ ما لَنا فِي بَناتِكَ مِنْ حَقٍّ): علمت is suspended from acting by the negative ما; لنا is a fronted khabar; في بناتك is a ḥāl because it was originally an adjective of حق but was fronted; من is a redundant preposition; and حق is a postponed mubtadaʾ in position. (وَإِنَّكَ لَتَعْلَمُ ما نُرِيدُ): the wāw is a conjunction; inna and its ism; the shifted lām; the clause تعلم is its khabar; and ما may be maṣdariyya or relative, i.e. "you know what we want" or "you know our desire". (قالَ لَوْ أَنَّ لِي بِكُمْ قُوَّةً أَوْ آوِي إِلى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ): لو is conditional; أن and what is in its scope is the agent of an omitted verb, its implied form being "had been established and settled"; as for Sībawayh, he sees it as a mubtadaʾ with no khabar, and the detail of that will come in the section on Benefits. أن is a particle resembling the verb, لي its fronted khabar, بكم a ḥāl from قوة since it was originally an adjective of an indefinite, and قوة the ism of أن. The response of لو is omitted, its implied form being "I would have done to you and made..."; أو is a conjunction; آوي is conjoined according to the meaning, the implied form of the speech being "or that I take refuge"; it is also permissible for the clause to be conjoined to the omitted clause ثبت if أن and what is in its scope is parsed as the agent of an omitted verb; and it is permissible that it be conjoined to قوة, because it was originally accusative by an implied أن, and when أن was omitted the verb became nominative, like His words «And among His signs He shows you» (ومن آياته يريكم); Abū al-Baqāʾ considered this view weak. إلى ركن is attached to آوي, and شديد is an adjective.
(قالُوا يا لُوطُ إِنَّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ لَنْ يَصِلُوا إِلَيْكَ): inna and its ism; رسل ربك is its khabar; لن is a particle of negation, accusative-governing, and futurity; يصلوا is an imperfect verb accusative by an implied أن; and إليك is attached to يصلوا. (فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; بأهلك is a ḥāl, i.e. "accompanying them"; بقطع is a ḥāl from أهلك, i.e. "accompanying a portion"; you may make the bāʾ one of transitivity, attaching it to أسر; al-qiṭʿ here is half the night, because it is a portion of it equal to the rest; the discussion of al-qiṭʿ has already appeared in Sūrat Yūnus; and من الليل is an adjective of قطع. (وَلا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنْكُمْ أَحَدٌ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ إِنَّهُ مُصِيبُها ما أَصابَهُمْ): the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; يلتفت is an imperfect verb jussive by لا; منكم is a ḥāl because it was originally an adjective of أحد; أحد is the agent; إلا is a particle of exception; and امرأتك is excepted from His words فأسر بأهلك; in one reading it is nominative, a badal from أحد, and a detailed discussion of this exception will come. The meaning is "do not take her with you, but leave her behind with her people"; and it is said it is excepted from أحد. Then inna and its ism, the hāʾ being the pronoun of the matter and the account (ḍamīr al-shaʾn); مصيبها is a fronted khabar; ما is a relative noun, a postponed mubtadaʾ; the clause أصابهم is the ṣila; and the sentence is the khabar of inna, because the pronoun of the matter is explained by a sentence whose two parts are stated. (إِنَّ مَوْعِدَهُمُ الصُّبْحُ أَلَيْسَ الصُّبْحُ بِقَرِيبٍ): inna and its ism; الصبح is its khabar; the hamza is for affirmative interrogation; ليس and its ism; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition; and قريب is genitive in form, in the position of the khabar of ليس. (فَلَمَّا جاءَ أَمْرُنا جَعَلْنا عالِيَها سافِلَها): لما is temporal or connective; جاء أمرنا: a verb and an agent; the clause جعلنا is the response of لما, نا being the agent; عاليها is the first direct object of جعل and سافلها the second direct object of جعلنا. (وَأَمْطَرْنا عَلَيْها حِجارَةً مِنْ سِجِّيلٍ مَنْضُودٍ مُسَوَّمَةً عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ): وأمطرنا is conjoined to جعلنا; عليها is attached to أمطرنا; حجارة is a direct object; من سجيل is an adjective of حجارة; منضود an adjective of سجيل; مسومة a second adjective of حجارة; and the adverbial عند ربك is attached to مسومة. (وَما هِيَ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ بِبَعِيدٍ): ما is the Ḥijāzī mā and هي its ism. There is disagreement about this pronoun: it is said it refers to the punishment understood from the context; it is said it refers to the stones, being the nearest mentioned; and it is said it refers to the destroyed towns; and all that they mentioned is permissible and sound. من الظالمين is attached to ببعيد; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition; and بعيد is genitive in form, in the position of the khabar of ما. It was not made feminine either because it was originally an adjective of an omitted place, its implied form being "and it is not at a distant place, but near"; or because ʿuqūba and ʿiqāb are one thing; or by interpreting the stones as punishment.

* Benefits:
1- Returning to «law»:
The discussion of law appeared in al-Baqara and elsewhere. Here we add the discussion of the noun occurring after the conditional law. It is well known that it is restricted to the verb, whether conditional or maṣdariyya, but a noun may follow it, in which case it is parsed as the agent of an omitted verb explained by what follows it. On this basis is explained the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to Abū ʿUbayda, when he was on his way to Syria and, during the journey, before arriving, news reached him that a plague had broken out there; he consulted about going toward it or returning to Medina, and they differed, then he made up his mind to return after a group of the Companions had advised it. Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ said to him: "Do you flee from the decree of Allah the Exalted?" ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said to him: "Had someone other than you said it, O Abū ʿUbayda! Yes, we flee from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah." Thus غيرك is the agent of an omitted verb explained by قالها, the implied form being "law qālahā ghayruka", and the response of لو is omitted, i.e. "we would have excused him".
Al-Ghaṭamish al-Ḍabbī said:
أقول وقد فاضت لعيني عبرة ... أرى الأرض تبقى والأخلاء تذهب
(I say, while a tear has overflowed from my eye: I see the earth remaining and the friends departing.)
أخلاي لو غير الحمام أصابكم ... عتبت ولكن ما على الدهر معتب
(My friends! Had something other than death struck you, I would have reproached; but there is no reproaching Time.)
Thus غير is an agent of an omitted verb explained by أصابكم, the implied form being "had something other than al-ḥimām struck you" (al-ḥimām, with kasra on the ḥāʾ, is death) "I would have reproached". Among the remarks of al-Tibrīzī on this second verse is his saying: People recite "akhillāy" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, as if they treated it as the shortening of the lengthened; but better by the rule of Arabic is to recite "akhillāʾ" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning "yā akhillāʾī", the yāʾ of annexation being dropped and the hamza left, as you say "yā ghulām". Also among such cases is their proverb «لو ذات سوار لطمتني» ("Had a woman wearing a bracelet slapped me"), taken from the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī when a slave girl slapped him while he was a captive among some Arab clans; so ذات سوار is the agent of an omitted verb under the condition of explanation, the implied form being "law laṭamatnī dhāt siwār"; the one with the bracelet (dhāt al-siwār) is the free woman, because slave girls among the Arabs do not wear bracelets; and the response of لو is omitted, the implied form being "the matter would be lighter on me"; or it may be accusative by an omitted verb or a khabar of an omitted kāna. An example of the first: "Had I seen Zayd, I would have honoured him"; and of the second, as in "Seek, even a ring of iron" (التمس ولو خاتما من حديد), which has already been mentioned.
It is common for the doubled أن and its ṣila to follow law, as in «And if they had been patient» (ولو أنهم صبروا) and the verse we are at, which is «If only I had power over you» (لو أن لي قوة). There is disagreement over the i'rab of أن and what is in its scope, after all agreeing that it is nominative in position. Sībawayh and the majority of the Basrans said: it is a mubtadaʾ with no khabar, or its khabar is omitted, the implied form being "and had their patience been established"; while the Kufans, al-Zamakhsharī, and from the Basrans al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjāj went to the view that it is an agent of an implied "thabata", as mentioned before, i.e. "had their patience been established". More of the rulings of law will come in other places of this book.

2- The statements of the grammarians on «illā imraʾataka»:
The second benefit is the statements of the grammarians on the exception of امرأتك. They said:
«ولا يلتفت منكم أحد إلا امرأتك» with the nominative in the reading of Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr, so امرأتك is a badal from أحد, a part-from-whole badal; the accusative is good Arabic and is among the seven readings, but is contrary to the preferred, stronger one, and the one more widely read. Hence al-Zamakhsharī made the accusative an exception from أهلك, so that it is an exception from a complete positive (statement), and the nominative a badal from أحد; and it was objected that this entails a contradiction between the two readings, for the woman would be taken along on the nominative reading and not taken along on the accusative reading. The supporters of al-Zamakhsharī answered that her exclusion from the sentence of prohibition does not indicate that she was taken along, but that she was with them, and it has been reported that she followed them. Ibn Hishām refuted al-Zamakhsharī's i'rab and said that it is contrary to the apparent sense, and he expanded on this exception in the second direction of the fifth chapter.
I say: the most apparent of all this is that the exception is from the sentence of the command, i.e. "travel by night with your family", and the exception is discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ) in both readings; the justification of the nominative is that it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the sentence after it, and in that case the accusative reading is good and not the weaker one, thereby avoiding the occurrence of the less preferred in the Qur'an. It has already been said concerning the son of Nūḥ «he is not of your family» (انه ليس من أهلك), because what is meant by "family" is the believers, and on this basis his wife is not of his family.

* Rhetoric:
In the words of Allah the Exalted: «Is not the morning near?» (أليس الصبح بقريب) is irsāl al-mathal or al-tamthīl (the sending forth of the proverb), a art that can be defined as what the speaker brings out running the course of current proverbs. It has already been alluded to and more of it will come. Our early scholars took pains to exhaust all the proverbs of the Noble Book, sūra by sūra in their order. As for Arabic poetry, we have mentioned earlier proverbs that the poet of immortality, Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī, included in his verses, and they came as a sign of originality, as we also mentioned a poem by Ibn Zaydūn. It is related that one of the shaykhs of al-Anbār in the time of al-Rashīd used to call the adhān and lead the prayer in a mosque, and when the time of the rose came he would hand the mosque's key to the people of the quarter, then plunge into the depths of his pleasure and not appear while there was a rose in the world. When he sat to his drink he would sing in a loud voice and say:
يا صاحبي اسقياني ... من قهوة خندريس
(O my two companions, give me to drink of old wine,)
خذا من الورد حظا ... بالقصف غير حبيس
(take your share of the rose, in revelry unrestrained,)
على وجينات ورد ... يذهبن همّ النفوس
(upon rose-like cheeks that banish the cares of souls.)
ما تنظران فهذا ... زمان حث الكؤوس
(What are you waiting for? This is the time of urging on the cups;)
فبادروا قبل فوت ... «لا عطر بعد عروس»
(so hasten before it is lost: "No perfume after the bride.")
